Five jumbled-up sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

2. This explains why, after Edward I came to the throne in 1272, negotiations went on for a number of years before Alexander III, King of Scots, performed homage to Edward for his extensive lands in England in 1278.

3. In the 12th and 13th centuries, when a king held land in another kingdom, it was unavoidable that he would have to perform homage and swear fealty to another monarch; this was awkward.

4. By the time Edward I invaded Scotland in 1296, Scots already regarded their country as a sovereign kingdom, exempt from paying homage to any other kingdom.

5. Homage meant a public act of acknowledgement of a vassal to his lord and had to be performed in person, compromising royal dignity for some kings.

This also marks a shift in political stance that does not fit with the discussion in the remaining statements. Though chronologically, we can link 2 and 4, the ideas do not connect; thus, sentence 4 is the odd one out here.

The commodification of self would seem to be a misnomer. If a commodity is a product, something that can be bought and sold, then in what sense can the self be commodified? Without any claim to being exhaustive, I want to discuss two possible meanings. A first is that self-understanding is mediated by the consumption of goods and images, self-definition depends on the appropriation of the traits of commodities. We know who we are and we judge the quality of our inner experience through identification with the things we buy. The second meaning involves the reorganization of our personal lives and relationships on the model of market relations. This adaptation is well illustrated by the recent practice of “personal branding,” a strategy of cultivating a name and image of ourselves that we manipulate for economic gain. Both of these meanings concern the terms in which we define ourselves and our well-being, and each has been facilitated by the loosening of self-definitions from specific social roles and obligations.

In the 1970s and 1980s a body of literature appeared documenting a modal shift in the way that Americans conceive of and express themselves. Compared with the 1950s and before, scholars argued, people now put less emphasis on institutional roles in their self-definitions and weighed more on internal criteria or “impulse.” The shift in self-conception, these writers argued, was fueled by ongoing social and cultural changes and was having important personal and public consequences.

In a characteristic article, published in 1976, the sociologist Ralph Turner found evidence that “recent decades have witnessed a shift in the locus of self….” He characterized the movement in self-anchorage—in the feelings and actions that we identify as expressions of our “real self”—as movement along a continuum from “institution” to “impulse.” At the institutional pole, one recognizes the real self in the pursuit of institutionalized goals. Self-control, volition, and exacting standards within institutional frameworks are paramount. At the impulse pole, by contrast, “institutional motivations are external, artificial constraints and superimpositions that bridle manifestations of the real self.” Though few people occupy the extremes, Turner emphasized, the personal relevance of institutions seemed to be declining and personal reality increasingly indexed to impulse.

Turner’s observations were not unique. Earlier, Nathan Adler had suggested that an “antinomian personality,” a character type who rejects conventional morality, was emerging for whom the expression of impulse and desire is central. Similarly, Christopher Lasch, in his bestseller The Culture of Narcissism, saw the spread of a “therapeutic outlook” in American society that seeks peace of mind in the “overthrow of inhibitions and the immediate gratification of every impulse.” Along with others, these scholars saw the sixties and seventies as giving rise to a new emphasis on the exploration of personal desires and immediate experience, on distancing oneself from institutional (i.e., external) norms and goals, on finding one’s unique inner voice, and on freely expressing one’s intimate feelings. None of these sentiments were new, of course; all reflect an old Romantic sensibility. Yet the evidence suggested that they resonated as an ideal and as terms of self-expression with a much wider swath of the public.

questions.question_text: Which of the following implications is most consistent with Turner’s observations in the passage?

options.label: A
options.option_text: Individuals who derive identity from institutional goals may view impulse-driven selfhood as dangerously self-indulgent.

options.label: B
options.option_text: The decline of institutions implies that most people will eventually embrace a wholly “antinomian” orientation.

options.label: C
options.option_text: Ideals of spontaneity and desire are incompatible with institutional definitions of self and cannot coexist with them.

options.label: D
options.option_text: Even when impulses gain prominence, many individuals may still partially define themselves through institutional roles.

questions.solution_text:
In the passage, Turner described a continuum running from “institution” to “impulse” in how people anchor their sense of self. He noted that while institutional relevance was declining and impulses were increasingly taken as markers of authenticity, very few individuals occupied either “extreme” of the continuum. Based on this understanding, let us examine the given choices -
Option A is speculative: it is plausible that if someone is anchored at the institutional pole, they might regard impulse-based selfhood as “indulgent,” destabilising or undesirable. However, this is not a definite inference we can make since there is no discussion on attitudes.
Option B goes too far in suggesting that the decline of institutions means most people will inevitably become fully “antinomian” (rejecting all external norms). Turner explicitly states that few people actually reside at the extremes, indicating that people might have a more moderate view of things.
Option C states that desire-based and institutional definitions cannot coexist. This is too absolute; Turner frames institutions and impulses as poles of a spectrum, not as strictly “incompatible.” More information would be needed to justify this assertion.
Option D aligns with Turner’s discussion since he emphasises that although impulses have gained prominence, many people still define themselves in part through institutions. His observation is not about replacement but about relative decline, which the statement here reflects aptly.
Hence, Option D is the best choice.

In a dimly lit arena in London, the crowd counts down from 20. Two athletes crouch inside a maze of bars and ramps, waiting for the buzzer. One will chase, the other will try to escape. The boom owes much to the COVID-19 pandemic. When mainstream leagues shut, locked-down audiences devoured whatever competitions remained. Nowadays, platforms like Netflix and Disney+ have unlimited schedules and global reach, giving small sports room to grow. That trend is visible in other corners of the internet: streaming has given worldwide distribution to niche varieties of content, helping local genres like K-pop build global fan bases.

Meanwhile, soaring franchise values have cemented sport as an asset class. Private-equity firms accounted for 45% of sports-industry deals in 2024, with the number of deals nearly doubling from the previous year. Yet entry to the top tier is scarce: stakes in mega-franchises like America’s National Football League (NFL) or National Basketball Association rarely come up for sale. That pushes capital towards smaller leagues. “Niche sports offer investors a foot in the door,” says analyst Avery Wright. By backing competitions from the ground up, investors build the credibility and experience needed for when established franchises eventually open to new capital. For funds that already own big-league assets, smaller leagues offer diversification and a chance to apply their expertise ... 

Upstarts are designed to reach young audiences. Established sports like tennis and golf are grappling with ageing fan bases. Freed from legacy rulebooks, newcomers can design their products to suit digital natives with short attention spans. TGL, a golf league founded by Tiger Woods that stages contests in indoor arenas with computer simulators, draws audiences 12 years younger than the PGA Tour, golf’s main circuit/league. The King’s League, a five-a-side football tournament founded in Spain in 2022, keeps fans engaged by letting them vote online for rule changes. Many of these contests feel more like festivals than fixtures; the party atmosphere at such events draws younger crowds.

The big question is how to monetise all this new attention. Smaller leagues rely on the same three revenue streams as the giants: media rights; sponsorships; and ticketing and merchandise. But the mix varies. Whereas about half the NFL’s revenue comes from broadcasters, some niche leagues charge little or nothing for media rights, preferring to maximise exposure. Social media is crucial: viral clips on TikTok or Instagram can quickly translate into jersey sales.

A flight away from cities towards rural areas also meant less circulation of infectious diseases. Finally, a more complex reason in at least some cases is a survivor effect. Some collapses did lead to population declines: sometimes death, but also because people moved.
